# Working on remote machines: `ssh`, `scp`, `rsync` and `tmux`

Big data rarely lives on your laptop. You work on a server or a cluster: a computer in a machine room that you reach over the network, with far more cores, memory and disk than yours. Everything you have learned so far works there too, because you give it commands through a shell. The tools below get you there, move the files, and keep your jobs alive.

(These examples need an account on a remote machine. Replace `user@server` with your own login.)

## `ssh`: log in to another machine

```bash
ssh user@server          # log in; the prompt is now on the server
ssh user@server "df -h"  # run one command there and come back
exit                                 # leave the server (or Ctrl+D)
```

After `ssh` connects, you are typing into a shell on the server, and `pwd`, `ls`, `htop` and the rest refer to *that* machine. Check which one you are on by the prompt or with `hostname`.

Typing a password each time gets tedious. A **key pair** replaces it: you create a private key that stays on your computer and a public key that you give to the server:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519                # make the key pair, once
ssh-copy-id user@server  # install your public key on the server
ssh user@server          # now logs in without a password
```

Never share the private key (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519`). The public one, `id_ed25519.pub`, is meant to be shared.

## `scp` and `rsync`: copy files between machines

`scp` ("secure copy") is `cp` across the network. The remote side is written `user@server:path`, and the colon is what says "this is on the server":

```bash
scp results.csv user@server:~/data/     # your computer to the server
scp user@server:~/out/model.pkl .       # server to here (. : this folder)
scp -r results/ user@server:~/          # -r : a whole folder
```

`rsync` does the same job better for anything big or repeated. It compares both sides and sends only what is missing or changed, so a second run of a large copy takes seconds, and an interrupted one can be resumed:

```bash
rsync -av data/ user@server:~/data/     # -a : keep folders, dates; -v : talk
rsync -avz data/ user@server:~/data/    # -z : compress while sending
rsync -avP data/ user@server:~/data/    # -P : progress, keep partial files
rsync -avn data/ user@server:~/data/    # -n : dry run, only show the plan
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The trailing slash matters
`rsync -av data/ dest/` copies the *contents* of `data` into `dest`. Without the slash, `rsync -av data dest/` creates `dest/data`. The same is true on the destination side. When in doubt, add `-n` first.
:::

# Beyond tables: unstructured data and data lakes

Tabular data is the easy case, because it fits a rectangle with a known type for each column. A lot of the world's data does not. People sort data by how much structure it has:

+---------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+
| Kind                | What it looks like    | Examples              | Tools in this course  |
+:====================+:======================+:======================+:======================+
| **Structured**      | rows by columns, a    | `covid.csv`, a        | `cut`, `awk`,         |
| (tabular)           | fixed type per column | database table, a     | `data.table`,         |
|                     |                       | Parquet file          | `pandas`, SQL         |
+---------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+
| **Semi-structured** | nested keys and       | JSON, XML, YAML, log  | `jq`, `jsonlite`,     |
|                     | lists; the shape can  | files                 | `grep`                |
|                     | vary from record to   |                       |                       |
|                     | record                |                       |                       |
+---------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+
| **Unstructured**    | no rows or columns at | photos, video, audio, | other tools: image    |
|                     | all: the content is   | PDFs, Word and        | and speech libraries, |
|                     | the file              | PowerPoint files,     | and increasingly      |
|                     |                       | scanned documents,    | machine learning      |
|                     |                       | emails                | models                |
+---------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+

: Three levels of structure. People often claim that most of the world's data is unstructured; that number is quoted a lot and measured rarely, but the direction is right, and it is the fast-growing part.

**Images, video and audio are numbers too, just not in a table.** A photo is a grid of pixels, each described by three numbers (red, green, blue). A 12-megapixel photo (4000 × 3000 pixels) is about 36 million numbers, which is 36 MB raw; a format like JPEG shrinks it to a few MB by throwing away detail we cannot see. An hour of 1080p video at 30 frames per second is about 670 GB raw (1920 × 1080 × 3 bytes × 30 frames × 3600 seconds), and video codecs bring that down to a few GB. Audio is a long list of loudness values, thousands per second. A PDF or Word file is a bundle of text, fonts and layout instructions.

**What is different about them?**

* **There is no "row" to cut out.** You cannot `grep` a photo for a county or `sort` a video by a column. The useful information (a face, a spoken word, a tumor in a scan) has to be *extracted* first, usually by a program or a model, and the extracted facts then go into a table.
* **They are big and each one is a unit.** You work with whole files, one at a time, not with billions of small rows.
* **They need a table next to them.** The usual pattern is a table of **metadata** (file path, date taken, size, who labeled it, the label itself) that points to the files. You query the table with the tools from this course, and open the files that the query selected. The files themselves are never edited in place, just stored, replaced or deleted.

**Where does all of this live? In a data lake.** A **data lake** is one big, cheap storage area (usually cloud *object storage*, such as Amazon S3) where an organization puts data in whatever form it arrives: CSVs, Parquet files, JSON logs, images, videos, PDFs, side by side. Unlike a normal filesystem, object storage has no real folders, just a flat set of named objects, and an object, once written, is replaced and not edited. (That is also why Parquet files are written once.) The contrast with the tabular world is the order of the steps:

+------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
|                  | **Data warehouse** (and a database) | **Data lake**                       |
+:=================+:====================================+:====================================+
| Holds            | structured tables                   | anything: tables, semi-structured   |
|                  |                                     | and unstructured files              |
+------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| Schema           | decided **before** loading (*schema | decided **when you read** (*schema  |
|                  | on write*): the `CREATE TABLE` in   | on read*): the file is stored as it |
|                  | the database unit below             | came, and you say what its columns  |
|                  |                                     | are when you open it                |
+------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| Cost per GB      | higher                              | low                                 |
+------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| Quality          | curated and checked on the way in   | raw. Without care a lake turns into |
|                  |                                     | a "data swamp": a lot of files that |
|                  |                                     | nobody can find or trust            |
+------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| Typical question | SQL on clean tables                 | anything, including training a      |
|                  |                                     | model on millions of images         |
+------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+

Newer systems blur the line. A **lakehouse** (Delta Lake and Iceberg, from the Parquet history in Lecture 3) puts a table layer, with types, transactions and SQL, on top of the Parquet files in a lake. So a warehouse-like table can live in a lake. A Parquet file is how *tabular* data is stored in a lake, and the database unit of Lecture 3 is the warehouse side.
